source_text: Alienos a fide abundare virtutibus, in quibus sine adiutorio gratiae, solum est naturae bonum, licet superstitionibus mancipatum, qui solis libertatis ingenitae viribus, et misericordes crebro, et modesti, et casti inveniuntur, et sobrii
pass_a_gloss: Alienos from fide abundare virtutibus, in to-whom without adiutorio of-grace, only is of-nature good, although superstitionibus mancipatum, who solis of-freedom ingenitae viribus, and misericordes crebro, and modesti, and casti inveniuntur, and sobrii.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'
LS libertas; Blaise moral freedom to will or refuse

pass_b_english: People outside the faith abound in virtues. In them there is only the good of nature, without the help of grace, although that nature is enslaved to superstitions. Through the powers of inborn freedom alone they are often found to be merciful, modest, chaste, and sober.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
In the suum cuique definition gratia is partiality, not saving grace.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
